Dr. C. Shepherd Burton, vice president and director of the Environmental and Information Management Services Division, oversees and actively participates in studies in the areas of atmospheric simulation modeling; risk and exposure assessment; regulatory review, analysis, and development; introduction and application of probabilistic methods in air quality management practices; visibility; and environmental statistics. His current work addresses most aspects of sulfur oxide emissions reduction in the United States. He is also involved in the development of national strategies for addressing ozone issues, EPA's developing indoor air and fine particle programs. He is among the principal architects and implementers of the expected exceedance approach to air quality management--a framework that provides more robustness and improved air quality management decisions; he has assisted the EPA to incorporate the expected exceedance framework into national ambient air quality standards for ozone and PM-10, and is currently active in the revision of the \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) standard. He serves on the EPA's Science Advisory Board's (SAB) Acute Toxics subcommittee; he is a participant in the SAB's review of the Superfund Hazard Ranking System; he is a member of the U.S. EPA's Clean Air Scientific Advisory Committee (CASAC) and Chairman of CASAC's newly formed Subcommittee on Visibility; and he has served on numerous peer review panels in the atmospheric sciences for EPA, NADPAP, DOE, and EPRI. On behalf of the Utility Air Regulatory Group, he functioned as participant and reviewer in the U.S.-Canadian Transboundary Air Pollution Working Group activities related to the suitability of atmospheric models for developing across-boundary emission control programs. Dr. Burton has participated in a number of workshops seeking to define future research needs in atmospheric chemistry and physics and to assess the roles and uses of air quality models in air quality management.

Prior to joining Systems Applications, Dr. Burton was engaged in laboratory measurements of fundamental hydroxyl radical hydrocarbon reactions. To perform these measurements, Dr. Burton developed a new technique known as variable frequency molecular modulation spectroscopy, which allows direct observation of the transient radical species. Dr. Burton holds patents for measuring real-time trace ambient quantities of ammonia, alcohols, and heavy metals using modulated excimer fluorescence and plasma spectroscopic methods. In addition, he was project scientist for the EPA Regional Air Pollution Study and project manager of the Navajo Generating Station  \( SO_{2} \)  field monitoring program, a study assessing the impact of a large isolated coal-fired power plant located in complex terrain.
